In [[graph theory]], a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G</math> is a '''pairwise compatibility graph''' (PCG) if there exists a weighted [[Tree (data structure)|tree]] <math>T</math> and two non-negative real numbers <math>d_{min} \leq d_{max}</math> such that each node <math>u'</math> of <math>G</math> has a one-to-one mapping with a [[leaf node]] <math>u</math> of <math>T</math> such that two nodes <math>u'</math> and <math>v'</math> are adjacent in <math>G</math> [[if and only if]] the distance between <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are in the interval <math>[d_{min}, d_{max}]</math>.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Rahman |first1=Md Saidur | last2=Ahmed |first2=Shareef |title=A survey on pairwise compatibility graphs |journal=AKCE International Journal of Graphs and Combinatorics |year=2020 |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=788–795 |doi=10.1016/j.akcej.2019.12.011 |s2cid=225708614 |doi-access=free }} {{CC-notice|cc=by4}}</ref>

The subclasses of PCG include graphs of at most seven vertices, [[Cycle graph|cycles]], [[Forest (graph theory)|forests]], [[complete graph]]s, [[interval graph]]s and [[ladder graph]]s.<ref name=":0" />  However, there is a graph with eight vertices that is known not to be a PCG.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Durocher|first1=Stephane|last2=Mondal|first2=Debajyoti|last3=Rahman|first3=Md. Saidur|date=2015|title=On graphs that are not PCGs|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|volume=571|pages=78–87|doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2015.01.011|s2cid=17290164 |issn=0304-3975|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Relationship to phylogenetics ==
Pairwise compatibility graphs were first introduced by Paul Kearney, J. Ian Munro and Derek Phillips in the context of [[Computational phylogenetics|phylogeny reconstruction]]. When sampling from a [[phylogenetic tree]], the task of finding nodes whose path distance lies between given lengths <math>d_{min} \leq d_{max}</math> is equivalent to [[Clique problem|finding a clique]] in the associated PCG.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Kearney|first1=Paul|title=Efficient Generation of Uniform Samples from Phylogenetic Trees|date=2003|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-39763-2_14|pages=177–189|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-540-20076-5|access-date=2022-02-13|last2=Munro|first2=J. Ian|last3=Phillips|first3=Derek|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=2812 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-39763-2_14 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Complexity ==
The [[computational complexity]] of deciding whether an arbitrary graph is a PCG is NP-complete.<ref>{{cite arXiv
 |last1=Dupré la Tour
 |first1=Max
 |last2=Lafond
 |first2=Manuel
 |last3=Ndiaye
 |first3=Ndiamé
 |title=Recognizing Leaf Powers and Pairwise Compatibility Graphs is NP-Complete
 |date=2025-10-22
 |class=math.CO
 |eprint=2510.19763
 }}</ref> Additionally, the related problem of finding for a graph <math>G</math> and a selection of non-edge relations <math>S</math> a PCG containing <math>G</math> as a subgraph and with none of the edges in <math>S</math> is known to be NP-hard.<ref name=":1" />

The task of finding nodes in a tree whose path distances lie between <math>d_{min}</math> and <math>d_{max}</math> is known to be solvable in [[Polynomial-time|polynomial time]]. Therefore, if the tree could be recovered from a PCG in polynomial time, then the clique problem on PCGs would be polynomial too.  As of 2020, neither of these complexities is known.<ref name=":0" />
